GodotCon 2026

Beyond the game

Developing your full end-to-end with Aspire

Maddy Montaquila · @maddymontaquila · @maddy.fm

Keep the opening familiar from the original deck, but do not explain Aspire yet. Welcome the room, establish that this is a game-dev talk, and set up the idea that the game is only the visible part of the system.

I just wanted to make a game.

Nothing else.

Let this breathe. The joke lands because everyone in the room has had a tiny feature turn into a pile of infrastructure.

It always starts simple

🎮 Game
Leaderboard Matchmaking Cloud Saves Friends Analytics Authentication
RedisPostgresDockerStorage ContainersOpenTelemetryMessage Queues APIsIdentityMonitoringSecretsCI/CD

...wait.

Click through each reasonable game feature. None of these are ridiculous. Then reveal the infrastructure cloud and pause. The point is not that game developers made bad choices; the point is that modern player expectations quietly require backend systems.

Then your morning starts like this

$ docker compose up
$ npm run dev
$ dotnet watch
$ godot --path .
$ redis-server
$ azurite --silent

This is normal now.

Play this as comedy, not complaint. Every terminal has a reason to exist. The absurdity is that we normalized needing a launch checklist before touching gameplay.

Game dev is full-stack dev

Players only see

🎮

Teams maintain

Leaderboards Matchmaking Auth Cloud Saves APIs Databases Containers Monitoring Telemetry
This is adapted from the original "Game dev is full-stack dev" slide. Keep it visual: players experience the game; teams own the invisible system that lets the game feel alive.

Games became distributed systems.

Do not mention Aspire. This is the thesis of the problem. Pause after the line and let people connect it to their own projects.

Modern apps

A big city without a map.

Services Databases Queues Auth Secrets Ports Telemetry Containers Deploy scripts
This reuses the original "big city without a map" idea but removes the dense lists. The emotional point is navigation: teams need to understand where everything is and how it relates.

Eventually I stopped asking for another script.

I wanted one command.

This is the turn into Act 2. Aspire should feel like the answer that emerges from the story, not a product being introduced first. 
> aspire run
game-api
leaderboard
redis
postgres
Dashboard
Health checks Tracing Logs
Reveal one capability at a time: services start, dashboard appears, then health, traces, and logs come alive. Keep it local-first. One command is the emotional payload.

Demo

Start the whole stack.

Show the repo. Run the command. Let the system appear.

Live demo beat one: run Aspire against the Godot sample. Do not over-explain architecture yet. Show that the loop starts from one place.

AppHost

The map.

var builder = DistributedApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

var db = builder.AddPostgres("postgres");
var cache = builder.AddRedis("redis");

builder.AddProject("game-api")
       .WithReference(db)
       .WithReference(cache);

builder.Build().Run();
AppHost is not "more config." It is the place where the relationships are visible in code. Use the map metaphor from the existing deck, but keep implementation details verbal.

Dashboard

My debugger for the entire system.

Health
Traces
LogsGET /leaderboard 200
cache hit
saved cloud slot
Relationshipsgame-api → redisgame-api → postgres
Avoid product terminology. It is okay to say the dashboard is powered by OpenTelemetry, but frame it as visibility from the beginning rather than a monitoring product.

Integrations

Building blocks. Not magic.

Redis Postgres Containers Storage Messaging AI Queues Existing services

Aspire works with the tools you already use.

This adapts the Integrations slide. The key message for GodotCon is that Aspire does not replace Redis, Postgres, containers, or your deployment platform. It helps you compose and run them coherently.

CLI

The one place I start everything.

> aspire run
> aspire add redis
> aspire deploy

One control plane for the local loop, without locking you into one cloud.

Mention open source, code-first, local-first, cloud agnostic, and OpenTelemetry here. Keep Azure out unless someone asks. This audience needs to hear that Aspire is useful even if their deployment target is not Azure.

What changes for game teams

Before

  • Did you start Redis?
  • Wrong port.
  • Missing env vars.
  • Works on my machine.
  • Docker isn't running.
  • Can't reproduce staging.

After

> aspire run
This reworks the original "What changes for game teams" content into an emotional before/after. The after column should feel almost comically small.

Demo

Break something on purpose.

Show how failures become visible instead of mysterious.

Live demo beat three: stop a dependency, misconfigure a path, or force an error. The payoff is observability during the inner loop, before players or staging discover it.

Spend your time making games.

Not infrastructure.

Close on the audience, not Aspire. The best ending is that the infrastructure fades back into support for the game.
